passages.t: A baby in a basket among the reeds
passages.happening:
“Now a man of the house of Levi married a daughter of Levi, and she conceived and gave birth to a son. When she saw that he was a beautiful child, she hid him for three months” (verses 1-2).

“But when she could no longer hide him, she got him a papyrus basket and coated it with tar and pitch. Then she placed the child in the basket and set it among the reeds along the bank of the Nile” (verse 3).

“And his sister stood at a distance to see what would happen to him” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Pharaoh has just ordered every Hebrew boy thrown into the Nile (1:22). This chapter answers that order with a marriage and a birth.

No one in these verses is named. A man of Levi, a daughter of Levi, a sister. Later the Bible gives the parents' names, Amram and Jochebed (6:20), and the sister is usually taken to be Miriam (15:20). Here the names are held back, so that when the child is finally named, he stands out. The verses also read as if this were the first child, but Aaron is three years older (7:7) and a sister is old enough to keep watch. The story keeps its eye on the birth that matters for what follows.

‘She saw that he was a beautiful child’ is in Hebrew, word for word, she saw that he was good. Many readers hear the refrain of Genesis 1, ‘God saw that it was good’, as if something new is beginning.

When she can hide him no longer, his mother does obey Pharaoh's order, in a way that turns it upside down. She puts her son into the Nile. But she puts him inside a sealed basket, among the reeds at the bank, where he can be found.

The Hebrew word for the basket is the same word used for Noah's ark. As the ark carried Noah's family through the flood, this little ark carries one child through the waters of death. Papyrus grew thick in the marshes of the Delta and was used for rope, mats and light boats, and tar and pitch kept water out.

The word for ‘reeds’ is the same word that names the Red Sea in Hebrew, which means the sea of reeds. The child placed among the reeds will one day lead his people through it.
passages.later:
Hebrews honors this mother and father: “By faith Moses’ parents hid him for three months after his birth, because they saw that he was a beautiful child, and they were unafraid of the king’s edict” (Hebrews 11:23).

Stephen says the same: “At that time Moses was born, and he was beautiful in the sight of God. For three months he was nurtured in his father’s house” (Acts 7:20).

The little ark recalls the great one. God told Noah, “Make for yourself an ark of gopher wood” (Genesis 6:14). Both times God carries life safely through water.
passages.asks: A mother did what she could and then let go, setting her child where only God could keep him. Ask what you are holding tightly that you may need to place in God's hands. And ask whether you can trust God with what you cannot protect yourself.

passages.t: Pharaoh's daughter, and a boy named Moses
passages.happening:
“Soon the daughter of Pharaoh went down to bathe in the Nile” (verse 5). She sees the basket and sends her maidservant for it. “When she opened it, she saw the child, and behold, the little boy was crying. So she had compassion on him and said, ‘This is one of the Hebrew children’” (verse 6).

His sister steps forward: “Shall I go and call one of the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?” (verse 7). The girl fetches the boy's own mother, and Pharaoh's daughter says, “Take this child and nurse him for me, and I will pay your wages” (verse 9).

“When the child had grown older, she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses and explained, ‘I drew him out of the water’” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Pharaoh's own daughter comes to the river. She opens the basket, the baby cries, and she pities him. Her words show she knows exactly whose child this is: ‘This is one of the Hebrew children’. She knows what her father has ordered, and she saves the boy anyway. The order to drown the Hebrew boys is undone inside Pharaoh's own house.

The text does not name her. No Egyptian record mentions her, so any attempt to name her is guesswork.

Then the sister, quick and brave, offers to find a nurse. Hiring a woman to nurse a baby was ordinary, and a child might nurse until two or three years old. Any Israelite hearing this would smile. Pharaoh's household pays Moses' own mother to raise the child Pharaoh wanted dead.

When the boy is older, he ‘became her son’. That is the language of adoption. A boy raised by a king's daughter would have been given the education of Egypt's ruling class. Stephen says Moses ‘was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians’ (Acts 7:22).

His name fits that setting. Moses is most likely an Egyptian name, from a word meaning ‘born’ or ‘son’, found in royal names such as Thutmose and Ramesses. In Hebrew it sounds like the verb ‘to draw out’, and that is the pun the princess makes. In fact the Hebrew form means one who draws out. The one drawn from the water will draw his people through it.

There is an old story from Mesopotamia, known from copies of the first millennium BC, in which the mother of King Sargon puts him in a reed basket sealed with bitumen and sets him in the river. Some scholars think Exodus uses a familiar kind of story. Others note that babies were abandoned often enough for such stories to arise separately. The differences are large. Moses' mother acts to save him from a death sentence, and his rescuer is the daughter of the very king who gave it.
passages.later:
Stephen tells it: “When he was set outside, Pharaoh’s daughter took him and brought him up as her own son. So Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” (Acts 7:21-22).

The rare verb ‘draw out’ is used of God rescuing the psalmist: “He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters” (Psalm 18:16).

Hebrews says that when Moses grew up he “refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter” and chose to suffer with God's people (Hebrews 11:24-25).
passages.asks: God saved Moses through a daughter of the house that wanted him dead. Ask whether you have written anyone off as being on the wrong side, too far from God to be used by him. And ask what it would look like for you to show the kind of pity Pharaoh's daughter showed.

passages.t: Moses strikes down an Egyptian, and flees
passages.happening:
“One day, after Moses had grown up, he went out to his own people and observed their hard labor. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own people” (verse 11).

“After looking this way and that and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid his body in the sand” (verse 12).

The next day he sees two Hebrews fighting and asks the one in the wrong, “Why are you attacking your companion?” (verse 13). The man answers, “Who made you ruler and judge over us? Are you planning to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?” Moses is afraid (verse 14).

Pharaoh hears of it and tries to kill Moses. “But Moses fled from Pharaoh and settled in the land of Midian, where he sat down beside a well” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The story jumps ahead. Moses is a grown man. Exodus gives no age, but Stephen, following the Jewish tradition of his day, says he was forty (Acts 7:23).

Verse 11 says twice that the Hebrews are ‘his own people’. The narrator makes plain whose side Moses is on. ‘Observed’ here means more than seeing. It means looking with feeling. He sees their burdens, and he feels them.

The Egyptian is ‘beating’ a Hebrew, and Moses ‘struck down’ the Egyptian. In Hebrew it is the same verb. Moses answers violence in kind. But notice how he does it: he looks ‘this way and that’ first, to be sure no one is watching, and he hides the body.

The next day his own people reject him. ‘Who made you ruler and judge over us?’ is bitterly ironic, because one day Moses will be exactly that. Moses calls the victim the man's ‘companion’, the same Hebrew word as ‘neighbor’ in the command to love your neighbor as yourself.

So the prince of Egypt runs for his life. He goes east to Midian, a land usually placed in northwest Arabia, east of the Gulf of Aqaba. The Midianites were descended from Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:1-2). He sits down by a well, and any Israelite knew what often happens at a well in the Bible.
passages.later:
Stephen's speech reads this scene closely: “He assumed his brothers would understand that God was using him to deliver them, but they did not” (Acts 7:25). Stephen then sees a pattern: “This Moses, whom they had rejected with the words, ‘Who made you ruler and judge?’ is the one whom God sent to be their ruler and redeemer” (Acts 7:35). In Stephen's speech the pattern runs on to the rejection of Jesus.

Hebrews praises Moses' choice of his people over Egypt's wealth: “He chose to suffer oppression with God’s people rather than to experience the fleeting enjoyment of sin” (Hebrews 11:25).
passages.hard:
Was Moses right to kill the Egyptian? The text tells what he did and gives no verdict, and readers have long disagreed.

Some see it as a just defense of a helpless man. The Egyptian was beating a Hebrew, perhaps to death, and the same verb for the Egyptian's blows and for Moses' blow suggests that Moses answered violence with the force it deserved. Stephen presents the act as Moses defending the oppressed and expecting his people to see that God was using him (Acts 7:24-25). Hebrews praises his choice to side with God's people.

Others read the details as a warning. Moses looked this way and that before striking, which suggests secrecy rather than open justice. He acted on his own, with no word from God. And his attempt failed. His own people rejected him, and he fled for his life. On this reading the chapter shows sincere zeal that was not yet shaped by God's call, and it takes long years in the wilderness before God sends him.

Both readings agree that Moses was right to side with the oppressed. They differ over whether his method was justice, or a rash act that God later redeemed. These notes do not choose. Neither reading makes this story a pattern for anyone today to take a life in secret; later in Exodus justice is set in the hands of appointed judges (18:13-26).
passages.asks: Moses saw injustice and acted, but on his own and in hiding, and it fell apart. Ask whether you have ever tried to do God's work without waiting for God. And ask what it means that God did not give up on Moses after his failure.

passages.happening:
“Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters, and they came to draw water and fill the troughs to water their father’s flock” (verse 16). Shepherds come and drive them away, “Moses rose up to help them and watered their flock” (verse 17).

The daughters go home to their father Reuel. “An Egyptian rescued us from the shepherds,” they say. “He even drew water for us and watered the flock” (verse 19). Their father says, “Invite him to have something to eat” (verse 20).

Moses stays, and Reuel gives him his daughter Zipporah in marriage. She bears a son, and Moses names him Gershom, saying, “I have become a foreigner in a foreign land” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Israel knew this kind of scene. Abraham's servant found Rebekah at a well (Genesis 24). Jacob met Rachel at a well (Genesis 29). Each time a stranger arrives, water is drawn, a young woman runs home, a meal follows, and a marriage comes of it. Moses fits the pattern. Like Jacob, he waters the flock himself.

This is the third time in the chapter that Moses steps in for someone weaker. The first ended in killing. The second ended in rejection. The third ends in rescue and a home. ‘Rose up to help them’ is in Hebrew ‘saved them’, the root of the Bible's words for salvation, from which the names Joshua and Jesus come. It is the first time the verb appears in Exodus. The man who will save Israel first saves seven women at a well.

The daughters call him ‘an Egyptian’. By his clothes or his speech, Moses looks Egyptian to them.

Their father is called Reuel here, which means ‘friend of God’, and Jethro in 3:1. Numbers 10:29 mentions Hobab, son of Reuel. The Bible does not explain the names. Some think one is a title, some that the family used more than one name, some that Reuel was the head of the clan rather than Zipporah's father. Zipporah's name means ‘bird’.

The son's name, Gershom, sounds like the Hebrew for a foreigner there. A foreigner in the Bible is someone living in a land not his own, with few rights. The prince of Egypt has become a foreigner, just as his people are foreigners in Egypt.
passages.later:
God had told Abraham his family would be “strangers in a land that is not their own” (Genesis 15:13). Moses now knows that from the inside.

Israel's law would later protect the foreigner because of this very memory: “You must not exploit or oppress a foreign resident, for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Exodus 22:21).

Stephen tells it: “At this remark, Moses fled to the land of Midian, where he lived as a foreigner and had two sons” (Acts 7:29).
passages.asks: Moses ended up far from home, a stranger with a son named for his exile. Ask whether you have ever felt like a foreigner, in a new place, a new church, or your own family. Then ask who around you is a stranger now, and how you might give them the welcome Reuel gave Moses.

passages.t: God heard, remembered, saw, and knew
passages.happening:
“After a long time, the king of Egypt died. The Israelites groaned and cried out under their burden of slavery, and their cry for deliverance from bondage ascended to God” (verse 23).

“So God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. God saw the Israelites and took notice” (verses 24-25).
passages.hearers:
Years pass. The king who wanted Moses dead dies. But the slavery does not end with him.

Three words for pain pile up: they ‘groaned’, they ‘cried out’, and their ‘cry for deliverance’ went up. The second is the cry of the oppressed calling for justice. Notice that the text does not say they prayed to God. It says only that their cry went up to him. God hears even a cry that is not addressed to him.

Then God becomes the subject of four verbs in a row. God heard. God remembered. God saw. God knew. After two chapters in which God has barely been named, the narrator makes plain that he was paying attention all along.

‘Remembered’ in the Bible does not mean God had forgotten. It means he acts on a promise he made. It is the same phrase used when God remembered Noah in the ark (Genesis 8:1).

Verse 25 ends abruptly in Hebrew. It says only that God knew, with nothing after it. The BSB's ‘took notice’ gives the sense. God knew their condition from the inside, the way someone who loves you knows. The ancient Greek translation reads differently here, that he made himself known to them, probably from a slightly different Hebrew text. Most English Bibles follow the standard Hebrew.
passages.later:
God says the same at the bush, in the next chapter: “I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out because of their oppressors, and I am aware of their sufferings” (Exodus 3:7).

Israel's law promises that God hears this kind of cry from the weak: if a widow or orphan is mistreated “and they cry out to Me in distress, I will surely hear their cry” (Exodus 22:23).

At the birth of John the Baptist, his father Zechariah praises God for the same faithfulness: God came “to show mercy to our fathers and to remember His holy covenant” (Luke 1:72).
passages.asks: God heard a cry that was not even spoken to him. Ask what groaning you are carrying that you have not yet put into prayer. And ask whether you believe that God sees you, and knows your condition from the inside.
